newsitem.title: THAILAND: Foreign bankers looking for Thais' next move.
newsitem.headline: Foreign bankers looking for Thais' next move.

text.p: Foreign bank sentiment towards Thailand now hinges on promised government measures to tackle the country's economic crisis and may depend on IMF involvement in a restructuring package, bankers said on Friday.
Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya on Thursday promised a package of measures within the next two weeks to help shore up the battered Thai economy.

"I'm looking for an announcement from Dr Thanong within the next two weeks and that might be that they are willing to accept some assistance from the IMF, the Japanese government, or some other foreign government," the general manager of Sanwa Bank Ltd in Bangkok, Hitoshi Komasaka, told Reuters.
IMF involvement in helping the Thai government manage the current crisis was increasingly essential, Komasaka said.

The Japanese government and banks have tied financial assistance to an IMF-sponsored package. The Thai government has so far declined to invite the IMF to organise a bailout and appears to want to arrange its own package.
Bankers said for that to be successful in restoring confidence it would have to include credible and concrete reforms.

"There is a lot of discussion that Thailand may borrow money from Japan, the IMF, or wherever. But whatever funding is raised will simply offset the continuing withdrawal of liquidity from the market as long as foreign creditors continue to have concerns," David Proctor, the head of the Foreign Bankers' Association, told Reuters.
Although onshore banks were continuing to respond to client needs in the interim, offshore banks were being more aggressive in restricting credit lines, Proctor said.
"I think there tends to be a difference between creditors with operations onshore and those banks who have been lending into Thailand from Singapore or Hong Kong or elsewhere," he said.
"It is clearly a lot easier for offshore banks to be more aggressive in withdrawing liquidity; I think for the onshore banks any withdrawal of liquidity simply hurts our own clients," he added.

Refinancing Thai corporates is increasingly urgent. At the end of the first quarter the central bank estimated corporate Thailand, excluding commercial banks, had some $29 billion in foreign debt falling due within one year.

Liquidity concerns have been exacerbated by the baht's de facto devaluation. Firms which failed to hedge their foreign loans now face higher repayments as the currency has weakened by about 25 percent since its flotation earlier this month. On Thursday the baht touched a record low of 32.70 per dollar.
In the short term the fate of $2-3 billion owed to foreign creditors by 16 ailing finance firms suspended by the central bank in June was weighing on creditor sentiment, Proctor said.
"The outcome of this is a critical first step to restoring confidence," he added.

Beyond a rescue package, corporate Thailand's chances of refinancing debts or securing new credit would depend primarily on the underlying fundamentals of firms and a company's relationship with its bankers, analysts and bankers said.

"Clearly for the economy there is substantial short-term funding supporting long-term assets and the economy does need a term out of this debt, but it really comes down to individual borrowers and individual client discussions," he said.
